historical_record.description: Designated San Francisco Landmark No. 201, Park Emergency Hospital.

The Park Emergency Hospital at 811 Stanyan Street, on the park's Kezar Corner, was built by park employees for $8,488 to designs by the city architect Newton J. Tharp — one of the few Beaux-Arts hospital buildings left, with sandstone walls and a red tile roof — and dedicated on May 15. The next morning its newly hired ambulance driver, James Wynn, was run over by his own bolting team as he unloaded supplies, the first member of the city's emergency hospital service to die on duty.

The earthquake damaged the Park Emergency Hospital; John McLaren put the repairs at $4,000, and a downtown businessman, Mr. Callaghan, whose gutted building had to come down, gave its stone to rebuild the hospital's walls. It reopened on July 15, 1906.
The city closed its Emergency Hospital Service, and with it the Park Emergency Hospital; the building stayed an ambulance station until the Paramedic Division moved out.
Closed for economy about a year after it reopened, the Park Emergency Hospital was used only as an ambulance base and renamed the Park Ambulance Station.
With the western city growing again, the Park Emergency Hospital reopened; from July 1911 to June 1912 it treated nearly 2,500 people.
